event.family_marine_01_before_dawn.choic: You clutch his sleeve. Your father stops in the middle of the motion.
You push his boots toward him. He realizes you saw the recall order.
You do not move. Your eyes follow every buckle, button, and movement.
event.family_marine_01_before_dawn.title: Before Dawn
event.family_marine_01_before_dawn.text: A recall order hits the door before dawn. Your father pulls his boots back on under the lamp. There is nobody else to stay with you when he leaves.
event.family_marine_01_before_dawn_i01_t: You tighten your grip. He has to gently pry your fingers loose before leaving.
You hand him what he forgot. He thanks you before stepping outside.
He meets your eyes, then looks down at the order as if he owes an explanation.
Your father pauses at the threshold, the folded order in one hand. Outside, the Marine waiting for him avoids looking in.
event.family_marine_01_before_dawn_i02_a: You refuse to forget that he left despite you.
You put away the rest of his things as if it were already your responsibility.
You remember the door, the lamp, and the sound of his boots.
The door closes. His footsteps fade before the room stops feeling too large.
event.family_marine_01_family_pennant.ch: You grab the blue cloth before the Marine finishes his sentence.
You immediately hand the pennant back to its owner.
Your finger traces the emblem's lines without leaving the cloth.
event.family_marine_01_family_pennant.te: A Marine from the neighborhood brings a small blue pennant for the household window. He sets it within reach while speaking with the adult beside you.
event.family_marine_01_family_pennant_i0: He laughs and says you already seem to recognize Marine colors.
He nods, surprised by your seriousness.
He names the emblem and shows you where it will be visible from the street.
The Marine crouches to take the pennant back, then pauses when he sees what you are doing.
The symbol quickly becomes something familiar in the household.
You watch the pennant as something that belongs to the adults first.
You memorize the emblem well enough to recognize it elsewhere.
The pennant is fixed to the window. Passing Marines recognize it at a glance; everyone else looks a little longer.
event.family_marine_01_no_box_on_form.ch: You stay put while he rearranges his equipment around you.
You push away the tool that keeps trying to force you into a measure that does not fit.
You watch the form while the clerk crosses out one box and searches for another.
You deliberately stretch your arm beyond the end of the ruler. The clerk calls someone else over.
event.family_marine_01_no_box_on_form.te: At the base family check, the clerk stops at a form designed for a Human child. Its chair, ruler, or boxes simply do not match your body.
event.family_marine_01_no_box_on_form_i0: Show what works
You show him where to place things so they stop getting in your way.
Keep the tool away
You refuse to let him use the old method again, even to save time.
Follow his new notes
You watch the words he invents to replace the crossed-out box.
Ask how far the string goes
The clerk unrolls the entire string. A quartermaster at the far desk turns around.
They Improvise
The clerk gives up on the standard setup. He fetches string, a second stool, and a blank sheet while the line waits behind you.
Look at the new entry
For once, the form changes around you.
Turn away from the desk
You leave after forcing the adults to respect a clear boundary.
Remember the correction
You mostly remember the moment the adult had to invent another way to do it.
Watch the quartermaster note your name
The quartermaster writes your name separately before handing the form back.
The Corrected Record
The clerk finally writes something that fits you instead of forcing the old box. The record goes back toward the base archives.
event.family_marine_04_empty_chair.choic: You push away the adult's hand when they try to take the chair.
You fold the chair yourself before the celebration ends.
Your voice breaks and several adults stare without knowing what to say.
They tell you a Marine cannot always choose. The chair stays empty.
The neighbor about to move the chair leaves it alone.
The small row around you agrees to keep the seat empty until the end.
event.family_marine_04_empty_chair.title: The Empty Chair
event.family_marine_04_empty_chair.text: Your father promised to be there for the neighborhood celebration. The benches fill, the second shift call sounds, and his chair stays empty.
event.family_marine_04_empty_chair_i01_w: You watch every uniform that passes at the end of the street.
You move the chair away so you no longer have to look at it.
Repeat it to anyone who asks
Every time someone asks, you give the same answer: he promised.
The celebration begins. Music covers the shift bell, but not the empty chair beside you.
event.family_marine_04_empty_chair_i02_t: You make him look at the ending celebration before accepting his excuse.
You are still angry, but you refuse to let his lateness erase the rest of the evening.
You head home before he can explain the mission.
Your father arrives as the benches are already emptying. He immediately sees the place you kept for him — or the one you put away.
You turn the box into a small job and stay near the wall.
You take the wrong passage and lose sight of the yellow line immediately.
You go too far before realizing you do not know how to get back.
You learn the rhythm of the corridors and move without being noticed.
You follow the base's movement while always keeping a route back to the storehouse.
The storekeeper gives you string and small tags to carry.
Nobody can watch you today. Your father settles you behind the base storehouse with a box of chalk and tells you not to cross the yellow line.
event.family_marine_04_you_come_to_base_: You become useful enough that the adults stop checking where you are every minute.
Keep going to the next corner
You push the exploration to where the corridors become unmistakably military.
People start recognizing you as “the storehouse kid” for the morning.
Boots keep crossing the yellow line. Every open door reveals a different piece of the base.
You follow the wrong coat and end up in a yard where nobody knows you.
A soldier brings you back to the storehouse before you find your father.
You spot the clearing passages and reach your father without obstructing the alert.
You anticipate the soldiers' movement and reach your father before he can come looking for you.
You stay exactly where you were left, even while everyone runs.
You push small crates and chalk out of the way so the adults can run.
A short siren sounds. Every adult suddenly changes direction, and the yellow line means little in the rush.
event.family_marine_04_dinner_interrupte: Pull him back to the table
You pull your father toward his chair. Your mother keeps her hand on the bowl.
Push his plate toward him
You push his plate toward his coat as if the choice were already made.
Say “Stay”
Your voice triggers the argument both adults were holding back.
Your father avoids your eyes and keeps hold of his coat.
Your father stops long enough for your mother to speak again.
Your father puts his coat back on the chair. Even the messenger waits for a different answer.
Dinner Interrupted
A Marine messenger knocks during dinner. Your father already reaches for his coat; your mother keeps a hand on his bowl and reminds him he promised to stay.
Stay beside your mother
Your father understands the cost of leaving before he even exits the room.
Hand him his coat
You hand him the coat. Your mother's silence grows heavier.
Ask who is right
The question forces them to explain what each had been demanding from the other.
Two Duties
Your father says the patrol is short-handed. Your mother answers that the household is too. The messenger remains at the threshold holding the order.
Accept that he goes
Your father leaves. Your mother stays beside you until his footsteps fade.
Ask him to stay tonight
Your father returns the order to the messenger and stays, at the cost of an explanation he will owe tomorrow.
Ask him to leave after dinner
The messenger agrees to wait a few minutes. For once, duty and family are not treated as an instant either-or choice.
The Messenger Waits
Nobody can pretend the decision is automatic: the messenger is still waiting, and dinner is getting cold.
event.family_marine_04_made_to_fit.choic: Show what gets in the way
You point out where the fabric pulls or blocks.
You test the fastenings one by one instead of making her guess.
You stand as still as you can while she works.
event.family_marine_04_made_to_fit.title: Made to Fit
event.family_marine_04_made_to_fit.text: A base seamstress opens the seams of a small practice jacket to adapt it to your body. She asks you to show her what gets in the way.
event.family_marine_04_made_to_fit_i01_f: You show her the exact movement that makes the jacket fail.
You suggest a different fastening instead of repeating the same setup.
You hold still a few more seconds before admitting it does not work.
The first version holds for a few seconds, then a seam pulls, a sleeve catches, or a fastening pops as soon as you move.
event.family_marine_04_made_to_fit_i02_f: The second version works because you helped shape it.
You move until you find the last weak spots, then she fixes them.
You let her apply what she just learned about your body.
The seamstress places the chalk in your hand and asks you to mark what she should change.
You take another piece of chalk and start a space beside theirs.
You force your way in and fall in front of everyone.
You step in, but the game stops around you.
You step in and refuse to leave. Eventually the game resumes.
You step in, move two markers, and show everyone another way to continue.
You stay outside the square and memorize their movements.
Children of Marines chalk out a drill square. When you approach, one blocks the entrance with a stick: “Not with this equipment.”
event.family_marine_04_off_drill_square_: Two children hesitate, then cross the chalk line toward you.
You stay there until someone agrees to resume the game.
From the edge, you copy a drill they just failed.
The other children turn toward you. The problem is no longer the equipment: they now have to decide what to do with your presence.
You describe the stick, the equipment, and the refusal. The adult has to answer something concrete.
You point to your own square instead of waiting for the adult to decide for you.
You give him no explanation. The group resumes, but the scene remains entirely between the children.
A Marine stops in front of the two chalk squares. He asks why the group is split before the other children can invent an excuse.
event.family_marine_04_quartermaster_mea: Stretch out both arms
You deliberately hold the pose and let him record everything.
Ask why
The officer cuts off your question and keeps measuring as if your opinion does not belong in the notebook.
He only says a Giant is “worth tracking.”
He admits some officers track Giant growth for military potential.
You keep asking until he explains what he records, for whom, and why your name matters.
Pull your arm back
You pull your arm back before the final measurement.
The Quartermaster's Measure
A quartermaster unrolls his measuring rope to the end, checks your reach, then writes your name in a notebook. At four, he already wants to know how large you will grow.
Look at the other entries
You realize this tracking existed before you and will continue after today.
Close the notebook
You place your hand on the page. The officer has to stop for the first time.
Point at your name
You make it clear you want to know why your name is there.
The Notebook
When the officer turns the page, you see other large measurements, ages, and notes about expected strength. Your name is not alone.
Accept testing, not deciding
You accept being tested, but not having your future decided for you.
Ask who decides for you
You refuse to let the notebook answer for you.
Refuse the tracking
You ask that your name not be used to prepare a career you never chose.
“Worth Tracking”
The officer finally says it plainly: some superiors want to identify Giants early who might one day serve in Marine forces.
Answer before your father
You answer for yourself. The officer writes that down too.
Let your father answer
You watch your father decide what he allows on your behalf.
Refuse yourself
You refuse clearly. Military tracking may continue elsewhere, but not with your consent.
In Front of Your Father
The officer finally asks your father whether he agrees to bring you back. This time, the question is asked in front of you.
event.family_marine_04_behind_office_doo: Press your ear to the door
The handle turns while your ear is still against the wood.
You catch a few words, then footsteps approach.
You understand the order concerns civilians your father believes would be endangered.
You hear the order, the refusal, and each man's reason before anyone approaches.
Call your father
You call him before hearing more. The argument stops behind the door.
Back away quietly
Your heel knocks over a bucket in the corridor.
You leave too late: your father spots you at the end of the corridor.
You leave the corridor unseen.
You leave silently and even memorize the route back.
Behind the Office Door
You wait in a base corridor. Behind the door, your father flatly refuses a patrol order. His superior reminds him that a Marine does not choose his missions.
Stay to the end
You stay long enough to understand the dispute is about specific people, not your father's pride.
Call him again
Your father finally opens the door. His superior immediately sees you were right outside.
Keep walking
You walk away knowing he said no, but not fully knowing why.
A Few Words Too Many
The word “civilians” carries through the door, then “risk.” Your father answers that an order can be lawful and still be wrong.
Ask him why
You ask him directly why he refused.
Pretend you heard nothing
You give him the chance to keep the argument to himself.
Say he was right
You take his side before he has fully explained himself.
The Door Opens
A few minutes later, your father finds you. He knows you were close enough to understand that he defied a superior.
Believe him
You discover that an uniform can contain refusal.
Ask what he risked
You understand his refusal could cost him something real.
Keep your doubt
You mainly remember that the same mission can have two different versions.
Why Did You Say No?
Your father finally chooses what to tell you: the order, the danger he saw, and what a Marine is supposed to do when the two no longer align.
event.family_marine_04_fallback_home.cho: You pull down the coat before it is soaked.
You deal with the overflow first.
You push the water back toward the door with whatever you can find.
event.family_marine_04_fallback_home.tex: Rain slips under the threshold while your father's service coat is already catching drops. The basin overflows and nobody tells you what to save first.
event.family_marine_04_fallback_home_i01: The coat is dry, but some floorboards are soaked.
You limited the damage by handling the most urgent source first.
Your arms tire before the rain does, but you kept the household afloat.
When the rain eases, the result of your first choice is obvious in the room.
You invent a difference and choose with far too much confidence.
You hesitate until the Marine takes both tokens back.
You spot a familiar scratch on the right token.
You spot the scratch and a wear mark the Marine had missed.
You immediately choose the wrong token.
You guess wrong and the Marine corrects you before the token leaves the counter.
You guess right without being able to explain why.
You guess right and the Marine laughs at your confidence.
You refuse to choose without proof.
At pay distribution, a Marine places two nearly identical tokens on the counter: one belongs to your household, the other to an absent family. He asks which one to take.
event.family_marine_04_fallback_service_: You leave with the right token and a better idea of how the base keeps its accounts.
You accept the written check over your intuition.
You memorize the detail that will let you rely less on someone else next time.
The Marine finally opens the pay ledger. Small notes beside the numbers explain why the two tokens look alike.
event.family_marine_04_fallback_adaptati: You gather what is nearby to make a place that fits you.
You let the adults move what is needed.
You refuse to be carried and stay standing beside the table.
In the base mess, the table reserved for families does not fit your body. An adult offers to carry you or move everyone else for you.
Nobody had to give up their place, and you did not need to be carried.
The adaptation becomes a shared task instead of a spectacle.
You keep your decision to the end despite the stares.
Benches scrape, trays shift, and every eye turns toward the solution you chose.
